1. The animation shows that the same fixed 2% raise protects a person's buying power very differently depending on when their 20 years of price changes begin. It uses three illustrative workers, each starting in a different month. Edna starts in Jan 1949, Ruth in Aug 2006 and Carl in Jan 1966. Each person's income rises 2% a year, and the rows of crates show how many goods that income buys.

2. Over the 20 years, each person's row of crates shrinks or holds steady as prices (US CPI-U) rise. Edna's row stays full at 10 crates. Ruth's row drops slightly to about 9. Carl's row drops to about 4, so his income buys much less than it did at the start. The frames also repeat that this is illustrative, US-only history and not a forecast.

3. A raise that stays the same can keep up with prices, fall a little behind, or fall far behind. What decides it is how fast prices rose during the specific 20 years. Carl's start date, Jan 1966, was followed by a period of fast price increases, so his 2% raise lost much of its purchasing power. Edna's period was mild enough that the raise matched prices. The video says this is past US history and not a prediction.

4. The video gives no explicit advice. A viewer could take away that income which doesn't adjust for inflation carries a real risk of losing buying power. That is relevant to your annuity quote, though the video doesn't mention annuities. Compare the two payout options with that in mind. For example, ask whether a payout that rises each year would protect you better than a flat one, and what the starting payment costs you for that protection. This is my inference, not something the video says.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The video's picture, on-screen text and narration only show how the outcomes differed by start date and say it is history, not a forecast. They don't recommend any action or mention annuities.
